decisions.body: How strong the evidence is: the analysis supports 470 Hz (a third of the loudest-partial energy of one Paris recording lies within 25 Hz of it) and reads the low note nearer 380 Hz than 340 Hz. It rests on two effective birds: one identified pigeon in Paris, 40 usable notes over two recordings, and four notes from Sangli. The two recordings of the same bird disagree on which partial is loudest. The analysis justifies no tolerance tighter than 8 % on either note, and that is the band of C21 and C22. Nothing has been printed or blown: a first print can miss by about 10 % either way, and a miss to the sharp side moves toward what the re-measurement reads.

inputs.description: Independent pitch analysis of the three coo recordings: F0 and loudest-partial tracks per note, spread, and how thin the evidence is

extractions.note: Supported by one recording of one bird; in the other two recordings 4 % and 10 % of the energy lies within 25 Hz of 470 Hz.
extractions.what: 470 Hz is supported: in recording XC539061 a third (33 %) of the loudest-partial energy lies within 25 Hz of it, and it equals the upper quartile of that energy (472 Hz). The measured top of the loudest partial there is 511 Hz (quartiles 455 to 533), 1.4 semitones above 470 (sections 0 and 5).

extractions.note: The low-note target of 340 Hz is the person's choice in the interview (R2), not a measured mode: this independent re-measurement reads the low note nearer 380 Hz. A 380 Hz low note is recorded as a rejected alternative of the pitch decision.
extractions.what: 340 Hz is weakly supported. It lies in the gap between the mode of XC541143 (295 Hz) and the mode of XC539061 (455 Hz): only 3 %, 11.5 % and 13 % of the loudest-partial energy lies within 25 Hz of it in the three recordings. 380 to 390 Hz has more direct support: the second harmonic of XC539061 starts and ends at 380 and 382 Hz, and the Sangli call sits at 388 Hz. 340 Hz is 1.9 semitones below that measured start (sections 0 and 5).

extractions.note: This 8 % is the band of the two physical pitch claims, and the reason the vent trim has to reach at least 50 cents each way.
extractions.what: The spread between recordings is far larger than the spread within one: the energy-weighted loudest partial is 292, 388 and 449 Hz in the three files (a factor of 1.54, geometric mean 371 Hz). A tuning tolerance tighter than about 8 % (1.3 semitones) each way on either note is not justified. A band of about 250 to 550 Hz, not two sharp frequencies, is what the evidence supports (sections 0 and 5).

extractions.note: 380 to 470 Hz would be 3.7 semitones, at the low edge of the rises measured (3.7 to 5.1 semitones).
extractions.what: The interval repeats better than the pitch: the fundamental's top over its start is 1.29 and 1.27 in the two Paris recordings (4.4 and 4.1 semitones), and the loudest partial of XC539061 rises 5.1 semitones (380 to 511 Hz). The targets, 340 to 470 Hz, are 5.6 semitones apart, a ratio of 1.38 (section 5).

How thin the evidence is: two effective birds. One identified individual in Paris gives 40 usable notes over two recordings six days apart; one or more unidentified birds at Sangli give 4 notes. Sex, age class and call type are not established, the recorders were hand-held with no calibrated level, and the two recordings of the same bird disagree on which partial is loudest. No published frequency for the coo of Columba livia was found (sections 0, 5 and 6).

extractions.note: The fundamental is the alternative that lost in the pitch decision: the person asked for the loudest part of the coo.
extractions.what: The deep fundamental of the coo runs about 190 to 240 Hz at the start and end of a note and 255 to 300 Hz at its top; the second harmonic runs about 380 to 600 Hz. Partial level falls to about -10 dB at 550 to 600 Hz in both Paris recordings. Near the top of the higher notes a component at 1.5 times the fundamental appears, which a pure-tone whistle cannot make (sections 0, 3 and 4).

inputs.description: Research notes with sources: support-free one-piece FDM whistles, print orientation study, windway and labium numbers, toy safety limits

extractions.note: Computed on a simplified shell without the voicing; no source compared windway orientations on one model with measurements.
extractions.what: Orientation: print belly-down with the tail on the bed and turn the voicing on its side, so that the windway is a vertical slot and the labium a vertical blade. Every voicing surface is then a perimeter wall and the windway gap, cut-up and labium offset are all dimensions in the layer plane. On the notes' simplified bird the bed patch is 2082 mm^2 belly-down against 198 mm^2 standing on the tail, and belly-down is the only one of three poses whose shell passes the pack's overhang measure at 45 degrees (sections 0 and 6).

Windway gap: draw 1.2 to 1.5 mm and never below about 1.0 mm. A slot between two perimeter walls closes by 0.1 to 0.3 mm in all, so add 0.10 to 0.15 mm to the drawn gap. A printed whistle head with a 1.3 mm windway works (section 2.1).

extractions.note: The growth is the notes' arithmetic. Whether a blunt 0.45 mm edge voices as well as a sharper one is untested there.
extractions.what: Labium tip: model an explicit flat of 0.45 to 0.50 mm, one line wide, never a knife. A slicer drops what is thinner than its minimum feature, so a knife prints cut short and the cut-up grows: 1.0 mm on a 25 degree wedge at a 0.45 mm minimum feature (section 2.1).
Elephant foot: the bottom 0.2 to 0.4 mm of a part bulges 0.1 to 0.3 mm, so the windway floor and the window's lower edge go 2.5 mm or more above the bed (section 2.1).

extractions.note: The 42 degrees of this design comes from the design panel, which found 43.5 degrees left no margin. The roof decision records what lost.
extractions.what: Chamber roof: the design rule is 45 degrees from vertical. On the notes' scratch body a round dome puts 6.4 % of the surface past 45 degrees (worst 79.9) and fails; a ridge tent at 43.5 degrees passes at 0.10 %. Each roof that keeps more than 90 % of the dome's volume needs a flat bridged strip 10 to 28 mm wide (section 2.3).

Bridges: sag is always present unless a bridge is under 5 mm (Hubs), so the top of the window stays under 5 mm or is chamfered at 43 degrees or less; the windway top is a 1.2 to 1.5 mm bridge and is negligible (sections 2.1 and 2.4).

Airtight walls: Prusa's water tests on printed cylinders find four perimeters the minimum for PLA and PETG. The notes recommend a shell of 2.0 to 2.2 mm made of 5 perimeters with no sparse infill inside the wall; five lines of 0.45 mm at 0.12 mm layers are 2.15 mm (sections 2.5 and 3).

extractions.note: The notes' own reasoning plus two maker reports; the design takes the second option, 5 perimeters with 18 % infill.
extractions.what: Sparse infill beside the airway is a leak path if any perimeter is porous: use solid infill in the thick parts, or 5 perimeters or more with solid top and bottom. Reported leaks in printed whistles are tied to infill under 20 % (sections 1 and 3).
Layers and material: 0.12 mm layers (0.10 to 0.16), and PLA for the first print, because PETG strings and a string across a 1.2 mm windway or the window is a voicing fault (sections 4 and 9).

Holes with a vertical axis print 0.1 to 0.4 mm small (the fdm-print pack's geometry rules; one user reports 0.23 mm) and one user reports them oversize on another machine: measure, do not assume the sign. Put the finger hole through a sloped part of the roof on a vertical axis (sections 2.4 and 5.1).

A closed chamber that leaks does not sound: one maker's guide says any micro-leak bleeds the pressure and kills the note (section 1, a shop blog with no measurements). Supports inside the chamber cannot be removed, so supports are off and the geometry must pass on its own (section 4).

extractions.note: A size rule only. The standards also test soaking, torque, tension and drop; none of that is checked here.
extractions.what: Small parts: the test cylinder of the toy standards is 31.7 mm across and 25.4 to 57.1 mm deep (EN 71-1 clause 8.2, ASTM F963, 16 CFR 1501) (section 8.2).

extractions.note: C26 keeps 90 dB(A); a reading between 85 and 90 has to be said out loud.
extractions.what: Sound limit: EN 71-1:2014 clause 4.20.2.10 holds wind toys to an A-weighted level at 50 cm of 85 dB when they imitate a musical instrument and 90 dB for whistles, with a C-weighted peak of 110 dB. The notes advise checking against 85 dB(A). No measured or expected level for this kind of whistle was found (section 8.3).

inputs.description: Research notes with sources: Helmholtz vessel-flute model, end corrections, published validation instruments, voicing rules, error band

extractions.note: Only the law is sourced. The model's three end factors (k_window, k_hole, k_vent) are calibrated on its own potential-flow solve and are not grounded by this input; k_vent 4.69 is far outside the textbook range.
extractions.what: Pitch law of a vessel flute: f = c / (2 pi) x sqrt(sum of G / V), with G = A / (t + k r) for each opening and r the equal-area radius; the conductances of the openings add (section 1.1: UNSW, Okada 2019, Csoka 2018). Exact corollary: f_open^2 - f_closed^2 = (c / 2 pi)^2 x G_hole / V, so the interval a finger hole makes does not depend on the window model. Textbook end factors k: 1.46 to 1.70 for a hole through a wall (sections 1.2 and 4).

extractions.note: Not measured on this whistle or this player: assumption C30.
extractions.what: Speed of sound to use: 346 m/s. A warmed, played wind instrument settles near 25.5 C (Fuks; oboe 25.6 C by Meyer, flute 26.8 C by Coltman); 346.1 m/s at 25 C; the humidity and the carbon dioxide of the breath roughly cancel. A cold first toot at 20 C is 13 cents flat, long warm play up to 17 cents sharp (section 1.3).

extractions.note: Not measured on a player: assumption C31.
extractions.what: Blowing pressure: with a 7 mm cut-up both notes speak at one pressure from about 100 to 650 Pa, and the best common point is 150 to 250 Pa (340 Hz is at its best near 130 Pa, 470 Hz near 250 Pa). These are computed from the Strouhal band, not measured; no blowing pressure of an ocarina in Pa was found (sections 1.4 and 2.3).

extractions.note: Measured on recorders, not on vessel flutes.
extractions.what: Jet band: a recorder head feeds its note while the Strouhal number f W / U lies between 0.07 and about 0.27 (Price; W the cut-up, U the jet speed); efficiency peaks at 0.14 to 0.18 (McKinnon's re-analysis of Verge) (section 2.2).

extractions.note: Sources are a 12-hole alto ocarina (Csoka), a soprano ocarina (Okada), a tenor and an alto recorder (Price and others) and one experimental organ pipe (Fletcher); none is a one-hole vessel flute at 340 Hz.
extractions.what: Voicing start values for 340 and 470 Hz, from published instruments and maker rules: cut-up 7 to 7.5 mm; windway exit 1.2 to 1.5 mm with the inlet about twice that; windway 20 to 35 mm long or more; 45 degree chamfers of 0.5 to 0.7 mm on both exit lips; labium edge on the windway mid-plane, 0 to 0.1 mm toward the outside; ramp 15 to 30 degrees; edge 0.5 mm or less (sections 0, 2.1 and 2.3).

extractions.note: The design's window is 7.0 x 6.3 mm = 44.1 mm^2: above the derived minimum, below the preferred range. The window decision records what lost.
extractions.what: Window size: the notes ask for a window as wide as the windway, 7 to 8 mm, and prefer 49 to 60 mm^2. Their derived minimum is a cut-up of 6 mm and a width of 6 mm, about 36 mm^2; they found no published rule (sections 2.3 and 6).

extractions.note: The notes' own synthesis of two measured instruments and several bottles; the source of the 10 % a first print may miss by.
extractions.what: Error band of the uncalibrated closed form on real mouth-blown ocarinas: about 10 % in frequency typical (170 cents), 15 to 20 % worst case, and the sign is not the same from one published instrument to the next (a thick-walled alto reads 17 % low to 3 % high by the choice of end factor; a long soprano 34 % high). The interval is much better: 1 to 3 % in ratio. After one calibration print, about 3 % (sections 0 and 3).

extractions.note: Computed in the notes, with no measured loudness of any ocarina behind it.
extractions.what: Chamber size for 340 Hz: 100 cm^3 or more is recommended and 125 to 150 cm^3 is comfortable; below about 80 cm^3 the window needs a deep neck and the whistle is quiet and breathy. By the notes' loss estimate 4.9 % of the oscillation loss is radiated at 100 cm^3, 6.4 % at 125 and 7.7 % at 150 (sections 0, 6 and 7).

Finger hole: sized from the interval law, about 6.5 mm for 340 to 470 Hz in a 125 cm^3 chamber with a 2.5 mm wall. 0.2 mm of diameter is 14 to 20 cents on the open note. Real ocarina finger holes run 2.7 to 9.8 mm (Csoka's ABS alto). No fingertip measurements were found; 7 to 8 mm for a child is the notes' judgement. Partial covering by arithmetic: a quarter of the hole open gives about 40 % of the rise (section 4).

extractions.note: No published limit for the ratio of chamber length to wavelength; the model's 0.10 and the claim's 0.125 are judgements.
extractions.what: Compactness: the wavelength is 1018 mm at 340 Hz and 736 mm at 470 Hz, so an 80 to 90 mm chamber is not negligible. First-order correction by the notes' own derivation: a window at the end of the chamber lowers the closed note 68 to 85 cents and the open note 125 to 155 cents; at mid-length 17 to 22 and 33 to 42 cents. The first lengthwise mode of an 85 mm chamber is near 2 kHz (section 5).

extractions.note: Arithmetic on the closed form, not a measurement.
extractions.what: A window shaded by lips or face (end factor 2.3 for 1.7) lowers the closed note 146 to 193 cents and the open note 74 to 96 cents in the notes' three worked sets (section 7).

extractions.note: The design goes one step further and prints the vent open, so that it can be plugged as well as reamed.
extractions.what: A small hole that stays open raises the closed note about twice as much as the open note: a 2 mm vent raises the closed note 98 to 159 cents in the worked sets. The notes advise to design the closed note flat and drill a vent to raise it, because lowering a note is hard (section 7).

requirements.statement: It looks like a pigeon: a chubby, cute city pigeon
It sounds like a pigeon: the same frequency as a city/feral pigeon's coo, matched to the loudest part of the coo, about 340 Hz rising to about 470 Hz

It is a toy, gift or desk piece: fun to blow and recognisably pigeon-ish; it does not have to fool a bird
